\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The empirical setting}

Consider a family of windows indexed by a parameter, and within each window a finite
set of \emph{hits} --- the positions at which some arithmetic or combinatorial
condition holds. To pool observations across windows of unequal length, one rescales
each window to $[0,1]$: a hit at absolute position $p$ in the window
$[j_{\mathrm{lo}}, j_{\mathrm{hi}}]$ is recorded at
\begin{equation}\label{eq:norm}
  x \;=\; \frac{p - j_{\mathrm{lo}}}{\,j_{\mathrm{hi}} - j_{\mathrm{lo}}\,} \;\in\; [0,1].
\end{equation}
The empirical density of the pooled coordinates $x$ is the \emph{positional profile}.
In the case that motivated this work --- the positional profile of the values
$v_j = j^2 - N$ across many choices of $N$ --- the profile had for some time been
summarised by a single decaying power law
\begin{equation}\label{eq:single}
  T(x) \;\propto\; (1+x)^{-b}, \qquad b \approx 1.104,
\end{equation}
fitted on roughly $10^4$ pooled hits from $\sim 10^2$ windows.

A tension appeared at the boundary. The share of mass in the \emph{left decile}
$[0,0.1]$ predicted by \eqref{eq:single} is $0.1415$; the measured share is $0.1620$
with a bootstrap interval $[0.1547,0.1695]$, so the prediction lies outside the
interval. A two-component alternative
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two}
  T(x) \;=\; A(1+x)^{-b_1} + K(1+x)^{-b_2}, \qquad b_1 \ll b_2,
\end{equation}
with a nearly flat bulk ($b_1 \approx 0.57$, interval $[0.41,0.77]$) and a narrow
spike carrying $\approx 8.6\%$ of the mass, reproduces the observed left decile
($0.1617$) and improves every model-comparison criterion decisively; matched control
data show no such component, and more than half of the improvement in residual sum of
squares is localised in the first decile.

Two questions arise, both mathematical rather than statistical: could a single measured
edge fraction ever settle the matter; and if a two-component profile is the truth, in
what precise sense is a power law wrong, and what is a fitted single exponent then
measuring? This paper answers both.

\subsection{Summary of results}

Write $\kappa_b(x) = (1+x)^{-b}$, $H(b,t) = \int_0^t \kappa_b$ and
$F(b,t) = H(b,t)/H(b,1)$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Closed forms} (Theorem~\ref{thm:closed}): for $b \neq 1$,
    $H(b,t) = \frac{(1+t)^{1-b}-1}{1-b}$ and $F(b,t) = \frac{(1+t)^{1-b}-1}{2^{1-b}-1}$.
  \item \textbf{Rigidity} (Theorem~\ref{thm:rigid}): $b \mapsto F(b,t)$ is strictly
    increasing, hence injective; and $F(b,t) > t$ for $b>0$.
  \item \textbf{Spike limit and non-falsifiability}
    (Theorems~\ref{thm:spikelimit},~\ref{thm:nonfals}).
  \item \textbf{Density-level separation}
    (Theorems~\ref{thm:logconv},~\ref{thm:nosingle}).
  \item \textbf{Mixture identity and effective exponents}
    (Theorems~\ref{thm:mix},~\ref{thm:inflation},~\ref{thm:exists}).
  \item \textbf{Cumulative-level separation and window dependence}
    (Theorem~\ref{thm:cumsep}, Corollary~\ref{cor:window}).
  \item \textbf{Left-edge steepening} (Theorem~\ref{thm:steepen}).
  \item \textbf{Spike-weight identifiability} (Theorem~\ref{thm:spikeweight}).
\end{itemize}

\section{The harmonic-type kernel}

\begin{definition}[Positional kernel]
For $b \in \R$ and $x \ge 0$ set $\kappa_b(x) = (1+x)^{-b}$. We call $b$ the
\emph{exponent}; $\kappa_b(0) = 1$ for all $b$, and $\kappa_0 \equiv 1$ is the flat
kernel.
\end{definition}

The shift by $1$ makes the kernel bounded and continuous at the left endpoint, so the
family interpolates between the flat profile ($b=0$) and arbitrarily concentrated
profiles ($b \to \infty$) without a singularity.

\begin{definition}[Head and tail mass; edge fraction]
For $0 \le t \le 1$ put
\[
  H(b,t) = \int_0^t \kappa_b(x)\,dx, \qquad
  \Theta(b,t) = \int_t^1 \kappa_b(x)\,dx, \qquad
  F(b,t) = \frac{H(b,t)}{H(b,1)} .
\]
\end{definition}

Elementary facts used throughout: $\kappa_b > 0$ and is continuous on $[0,\infty)$,
hence integrable on compacts; $H(b,t) > 0$ for $t>0$; $\Theta(b,t) > 0$ for $t<1$;
$H(b,t)+\Theta(b,t) = H(b,1)$. Two structural identities do the real work:
\begin{align}
  \kappa_{b+c}(x) &= \kappa_b(x)\,\kappa_c(x), \label{eq:addexp}\\
  c \ge 0 &\implies \kappa_c \text{ antitone}, \qquad
  c > 0 \implies \kappa_c \text{ strictly antitone.} \label{eq:anti}
\end{align}

\begin{theorem}[Closed forms]\label{thm:closed}
For $b \neq 1$ and $t \ge 0$,
\[
  H(b,t) = \frac{(1+t)^{1-b}-1}{1-b},
  \qquad\text{and for } 0 \le t \le 1, \quad
  F(b,t) = \frac{(1+t)^{1-b}-1}{2^{\,1-b}-1}.
\]
Moreover $H(0,t) = F(0,t) = t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The map $y \mapsto \big((1+y)^{1-b}-1\big)/(1-b)$ is differentiable on $[0,\infty)$
with derivative $(1+y)^{-b} = \kappa_b(y)$, by the chain rule for real powers of the
positive base $1+y$ and division by the nonzero constant $1-b$. Since $\kappa_b$ is
continuous, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives the first formula; dividing the
value at $t$ by the value at $1$ cancels $1-b$ and yields the second. Positivity of
$H(b,1)$ guarantees $2^{1-b}-1 \neq 0$.
\end{proof}

The excluded case $b=1$ is logarithmic, $H(1,t) = \log(1+t)$; every statement below
either avoids it explicitly or is proved without the closed form.

\section{Rigidity of the single-law family}

\begin{lemma}[Head discount]\label{lem:head}
For $c \ge 0$ and $t \ge 0$, $\;\kappa_c(t)H(b,t) \le H(b+c,t)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By \eqref{eq:addexp}, $\kappa_{b+c}(x) = \kappa_b(x)\kappa_c(x)$, and by
\eqref{eq:anti} $\kappa_c(x) \ge \kappa_c(t)$ on $[0,t]$. Integrate the resulting
pointwise bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Strict tail discount]\label{lem:tail}
For $c > 0$ and $0 \le t < 1$, $\;\Theta(b+c,t) < \kappa_c(t)\Theta(b,t)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Split the tail at $m = (t+1)/2$. On $[t,m]$ the bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:head} gives
$\int_t^m \kappa_{b+c} \le \kappa_c(t)\int_t^m \kappa_b$. On $[m,1]$ strict
antitonicity gives the strictly smaller factor $\kappa_c(m) < \kappa_c(t)$, so
$\int_m^1 \kappa_{b+c} \le \kappa_c(m)\int_m^1 \kappa_b < \kappa_c(t)\int_m^1\kappa_b$,
using $\int_m^1 \kappa_b > 0$. Add the pieces.
\end{proof}

The asymmetry --- weak on the head, strict on the tail --- is the wedge producing
strict monotonicity of the ratio.

\begin{theorem}[Rigidity]\label{thm:rigid}
For $0 < t < 1$ and $b_1 < b_2$ one has $F(b_1,t) < F(b_2,t)$. Consequently
$b \mapsto F(b,t)$ is injective: a power-law exponent is identified by a single
edge-mass measurement.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $b_2 = b_1 + c$, $c>0$, and abbreviate $H_1 = H(b_1,t)$, $H_2 = H(b_1+c,t)$,
$\Theta_1 = \Theta(b_1,t)$, $\Theta_2 = \Theta(b_1+c,t)$. Since
$H(b,1) = H(b,t)+\Theta(b,t)$, the claim is equivalent to
$H_1\Theta_2 < H_2\Theta_1$ after clearing positive denominators. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:tail}, $H_1\Theta_2 < \kappa_c(t)H_1\Theta_1$, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:head}, $\kappa_c(t)H_1\Theta_1 \le H_2\Theta_1$. Injectivity follows by
trichotomy.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Left over-weighting]\label{cor:overweight}
For $b>0$ and $0<t<1$, $F(b,t) > t$, with equality precisely at $b=0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:rigid} with $b_1 = 0$, $b_2 = b$, and use $F(0,t) = t$.
\end{proof}

\section{The spike limit and non-falsifiability}

\begin{theorem}[Spike limit]\label{thm:spikelimit}
For every $t>0$, $F(b,t) \to 1$ as $b \to \infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $b>1$ use Theorem~\ref{thm:closed}. Since $1+t>1$ and $2>1$ and the exponent
$1-b \to -\infty$, both $(1+t)^{1-b}$ and $2^{1-b}$ tend to $0$; the quotient tends to
$(0-1)/(0-1) = 1$, the limit of the denominator being nonzero.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Continuity in the exponent]\label{lem:cont}
For fixed $t \ge 0$, the map $b \mapsto F(b,t)$ is continuous on $(1,\infty)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
On $(1,\infty)$ the closed form applies; numerator and denominator are compositions of
continuous maps, and $2^{1-b}-1 \neq 0$ there because $b>1$ forces $2^{1-b} < 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Non-falsifiability of a single measurement]\label{thm:nonfals}
Let $t>0$, $b_0 > 1$, and $F(b_0,t) < \alpha < 1$. Then there is $b > b_0$ with
$F(b,t) = \alpha$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:spikelimit} choose $B > b_0$ with $F(B,t) > \alpha$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:cont}, $F(\cdot,t)$ is continuous on $[b_0,B] \subset (1,\infty)$, and
$\alpha$ lies between the endpoint values; apply the intermediate value theorem. The
endpoint $b = b_0$ is excluded since $F(b_0,t) < \alpha$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
No left-decile measurement, however discrepant, is by itself evidence against the
power-law hypothesis. In the motivating data the reference exponent $1.104$ predicts
$F = 0.14181$ and the measurement is $0.1620$; the exponent $b \approx 1.5698$
reproduces the measurement exactly. Detecting two-component structure therefore
requires a comparison of shapes across windows.
\end{remark}

\section{Two-component profiles and their separation from power laws}

\begin{definition}
For $A,K>0$ and exponents $b_1,b_2$ the \emph{two-component profile} is
\[
  T_{A,K,b_1,b_2}(x) \;=\; A\kappa_{b_1}(x) + K\kappa_{b_2}(x), \qquad x \ge 0,
\]
called \emph{genuine} when $A,K>0$ and $b_1 \neq b_2$. In the application $b_1$ is the
\emph{bulk} exponent (small) and $b_2$ the \emph{spike} exponent (large).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Geometric triple]
Positions $x_0 < x_1 < x_2$ in $[0,\infty)$ form a \emph{geometric triple} if
$(1+x_1)^2 = (1+x_0)(1+x_2)$; equivalently, the logarithms $\log(1+x_i)$ are in
arithmetic progression.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Power laws are log-affine]\label{lem:logaffine}
On any geometric triple and for any exponent $\beta$,
$\kappa_\beta(x_1)^2 = \kappa_\beta(x_0)\kappa_\beta(x_2)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\kappa_\beta(x_1)^2 = \big((1+x_1)^2\big)^{-\beta}
 = \big((1+x_0)(1+x_2)\big)^{-\beta} = \kappa_\beta(x_0)\kappa_\beta(x_2)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict multiplicative convexity]\label{thm:logconv}
Let $A,K>0$, $b_1 \neq b_2$, and let $x_0<x_1<x_2$ be a geometric triple with
$x_0 \ge 0$. Then $T(x_1)^2 < T(x_0)T(x_2)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $a = \kappa_{b_1}(x_0)$, $a' = \kappa_{b_1}(x_2)$, $k = \kappa_{b_2}(x_0)$,
$k' = \kappa_{b_2}(x_2)$, $p = \kappa_{b_1}(x_1)$, $q = \kappa_{b_2}(x_1)$, all
positive. Lemma~\ref{lem:logaffine} gives $p^2 = aa'$ and $q^2 = kk'$, so expanding,
\[
  T(x_0)T(x_2) - T(x_1)^2 = A^2(aa'-p^2) + K^2(kk'-q^2) + AK(ak'+ka'-2pq)
  = AK\,(ak'+ka'-2pq).
\]
The cross terms satisfy $(ak')(ka') = (aa')(kk') = (pq)^2$, so $pq$ is their geometric
mean; by strict AM--GM it suffices that $ak' \neq ka'$. For $c_1 < c_2$,
\[
  \kappa_{c_1}(x_0)\kappa_{c_2}(x_2) < \kappa_{c_2}(x_0)\kappa_{c_1}(x_2),
\]
since dividing by $\kappa_{c_1}(x_0)\kappa_{c_1}(x_2)>0$ reduces the claim to
$(1+x_2)^{-(c_2-c_1)} < (1+x_0)^{-(c_2-c_1)}$, true because $x_0<x_2$ and the exponent
is negative. Applying this with $(c_1,c_2) = (b_1,b_2)$ or $(b_2,b_1)$ according to the
sign of $b_2-b_1$ gives $ak' \neq ka'$, hence $2pq < ak'+ka'$ and the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No single power law on any subwindow]\label{thm:nosingle}
Let $A,K>0$, $b_1 \neq b_2$, and $0 \le s < e$. There are no constants $C,b$ with
$T(x) = C\kappa_b(x)$ for all $x \in [s,e]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Put $x_1 = \sqrt{(1+s)(1+e)}-1$, so $s < x_1 < e$ and $(s,x_1,e)$ is a geometric
triple. Theorem~\ref{thm:logconv} gives $T(x_1)^2 < T(s)T(e)$, while $T = C\kappa_b$ on
$[s,e]$ together with Lemma~\ref{lem:logaffine} forces equality. Contradiction.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:nosingle} is the falsifiability statement of the programme: if the true
profile is a genuine mixture, a pure power law is wrong on every nondegenerate
subwindow, and any future shape model must fail log-affinity on geometric triples. A
self-contained special case is the triple $(0,\sqrt2-1,1)$ inside the full window.

\section{The mixture identity and effective exponents}

\begin{definition}[Two-point mixture]
For $w \in \R$ put
$M_w(b_1,b_2,t) = (1-w)F(b_1,t) + wF(b_2,t)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Mixture identity]\label{thm:mix}
For $A,K>0$ and $0 \le t \le 1$,
\[
  \frac{\int_0^t T}{\int_0^1 T} = M_w(b_1,b_2,t),
  \qquad w = \frac{K\,H(b_2,1)}{A\,H(b_1,1) + K\,H(b_2,1)} \in (0,1).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Linearity gives $\int_0^s T = AH(b_1,s) + KH(b_2,s)$. Substituting at $s=t$ and $s=1$,
dividing, and writing $H(b_i,t) = F(b_i,t)H(b_i,1)$ exhibits the quotient as the stated
convex combination; positivity of $A,K$ and of the head masses places $w$ in $(0,1)$.
\end{proof}

Thus the observable normalised profile depends on $(A,K)$ only through the scalar $w$:
four parameters collapse to three.

\begin{proposition}[Strict bracketing]\label{prop:bracket}
Let $b_1<b_2$ and $0<t<1$. If $w>0$ then $F(b_1,t) < M_w(b_1,b_2,t)$; if $w<1$ then
$M_w(b_1,b_2,t) < F(b_2,t)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from $F(b_1,t) < F(b_2,t)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:rigid}) and affine interpolation.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Effective-exponent inflation]\label{thm:inflation}
Let $0<w<1$, $b_1<b_2$, $0<t<1$, and suppose $F(b,t) = M_w(b_1,b_2,t)$. Then
$b_1 < b < b_2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket} gives $F(b_1,t) < F(b,t) < F(b_2,t)$. Strict monotonicity
in the exponent (Theorem~\ref{thm:rigid}) converts these into $b_1<b<b_2$: $b \le b_1$
or $b \ge b_2$ would contradict one of the strict inequalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Existence of the effective exponent]\label{thm:exists}
If $0<w<1$, $1<b_1<b_2$ and $0<t<1$, there exists $b>b_1$ with
$F(b,t) = M_w(b_1,b_2,t)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The target exceeds $F(b_1,t)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket} and is below $1$,
being a convex combination of $F(b_1,t),F(b_2,t) < 1$ (each edge fraction is
$<1$ for $t<1$ because the tail mass is positive). Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:nonfals}
with reference exponent $b_1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Fitting a single law to a profile with bulk exponent $\approx 0.57$ and a very steep
spike necessarily returns a value strictly between the two; the historically reported
$\approx 1.10$ is that compromise. The pooled exponent is a statistic of the mixture,
not a slope of anything.
\end{remark}

\section{Window dependence: separation at the cumulative level}

\begin{lemma}[Differentiating in the window]\label{lem:diff}
For $t>0$ the map $s \mapsto H(\beta,s)$ is differentiable at $t$ with derivative
$\kappa_\beta(t)$; hence $s \mapsto F(\beta,s)$ has derivative
$\kappa_\beta(t)/H(\beta,1)$ at $t$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\kappa_\beta$ is continuous at $t$ and locally integrable, so the fundamental theorem
of calculus for the upper limit applies; divide by the constant $H(\beta,1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cumulative separation]\label{thm:cumsep}
Let $0<w<1$ and $b_1 \neq b_2$. There is no exponent $b$ with
$M_w(b_1,b_2,t) = F(b,t)$ for all $t \in (0,1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Suppose such a $b$ existed. Differentiating at each $t \in (0,1)$ --- legitimate by
Lemma~\ref{lem:diff} and uniqueness of derivatives for functions agreeing on a
neighbourhood --- gives
\[
  \underbrace{\frac{1-w}{H(b_1,1)}}_{=:A}\kappa_{b_1}(t)
  + \underbrace{\frac{w}{H(b_2,1)}}_{=:K}\kappa_{b_2}(t)
  = \frac{1}{H(b,1)}\kappa_b(t) \qquad (0<t<1),
\]
with $A,K>0$. This says the genuine two-component profile $T_{A,K,b_1,b_2}$ coincides
with a rescaled single kernel on $[\tfrac14,\tfrac34]$, contradicting
Theorem~\ref{thm:nosingle}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Window dependence of the fitted exponent]\label{cor:window}
Let $0<w<1$, $b_1 \neq b_2$, and let $b_{\mathrm{eff}} : (0,1) \to \R$ satisfy
$F(b_{\mathrm{eff}}(t),t) = M_w(b_1,b_2,t)$ for all $t \in (0,1)$. Then
$b_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is not constant.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
A constant value would exhibit a single exponent reproducing the mixture edge fraction
at every window, contradicting Theorem~\ref{thm:cumsep}.
\end{proof}

By Theorem~\ref{thm:exists} such a function exists (and is unique by rigidity) whenever
$1<b_1<b_2$, so Corollary~\ref{cor:window} is not vacuous: the fitted exponent is a
genuine, well-defined, non-constant function of the fitting window. This is the formal
content of the observation that refitting a single law on a narrower left window
returns a different exponent --- empirically, a steepening from $\approx 1.10$ on the
full window to $\approx 1.80$ on the left half.

\section{Directionality: the measured slope steepens toward the edge}

\begin{definition}[Measured local exponent]
For a positive profile $f$ and $0 \le x < y$,
\[
  \lambda_f(x,y) = -\,\frac{\log f(y) - \log f(x)}{\log(1+y) - \log(1+x)} .
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Scale-freeness of a power law]\label{prop:scalefree}
For $C>0$ and any $b$, $\lambda_{C\kappa_b}(x,y) = b$ for all $0 \le x < y$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$\log(C\kappa_b(z)) = \log C - b\log(1+z)$, so the numerator equals
$b\big(\log(1+y)-\log(1+x)\big)$ up to sign.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Left-edge steepening]\label{thm:steepen}
Let $A,K>0$, $b_1 \neq b_2$, and let $x_0<x_1<x_2$ be a geometric triple with
$x_0 \ge 0$. Then $\lambda_T(x_1,x_2) < \lambda_T(x_0,x_1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Because the triple is geometric, the log-spacings coincide:
$\log(1+x_1)-\log(1+x_0) = \log(1+x_2)-\log(1+x_1) =: \delta > 0$. Both local exponents
therefore have the same positive denominator $\delta$, and the claim reduces to
$2\log T(x_1) < \log T(x_0) + \log T(x_2)$. Taking logarithms in the strict inequality
$T(x_1)^2 < T(x_0)T(x_2)$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:logconv} --- valid since $T>0$ and $\log$
is strictly increasing --- gives exactly this.
\end{proof}

The drift of Corollary~\ref{cor:window} thus has a sign: as the measurement window moves
left, the reported exponent strictly increases. A single-law analysis of a
bulk-plus-spike profile is systematically biased in a known direction, and the size of
the bias is itself a diagnostic.

\section{Identifiability of the spike: weight yes, exponent no}

\begin{theorem}[Narrow-spike limit]\label{thm:spikeweight}
For fixed $w$, $b_1$ and $t>0$,
\[
  M_w(b_1,b_2,t) \;\xrightarrow[\;b_2 \to \infty\;]{}\; (1-w)F(b_1,t) + w .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$M_w(b_1,b_2,t) = (1-w)F(b_1,t) + wF(b_2,t)$ and $F(b_2,t) \to 1$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:spikelimit}.
\end{proof}

Two consequences pull in opposite directions. \emph{The weight is identified}:
rearranging, $w = \big(M_\infty - F(b_1,t)\big)/\big(1 - F(b_1,t)\big)$, the excess of
the observed edge mass over the bulk prediction normalised by the maximum possible
excess. \emph{The spike exponent is not}: the limit does not involve $b_2$, and by
Theorem~\ref{thm:rigid} the approach is monotone, so all sufficiently steep spikes
produce nearly identical observable profiles. Numerically, at $t=0.1$, $w = 0.086$,
$b_1 = 0.573$, the mixture edge fractions for $b_2 = 50$ and $b_2 = 2000$ are $0.19542$
and $0.19622$.

This explains an apparent pathology of the empirical fit: given a ceiling on the spike
exponent the optimiser saturates it; raising the ceiling from $10$ to $40$ produces an
interior optimum near $22.5$ with bootstrap interval roughly $[11,41]$, and the model
improvement grows. The likelihood surface is asymptotically flat in $b_2$, so the
correct report is a lower bound on the spike exponent together with a point estimate of
the weight.

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Edge-fraction inversion}
Given $t \in (0,1)$ and a target $\alpha \in (0,1)$, find the unique $b$ with
$F(b,t) = \alpha$. Rigidity makes $F(\cdot,t)$ strictly increasing, so bisection
converges unconditionally, and the spike limit guarantees a bracketing interval exists
whenever $t < \alpha < 1$. Cost: $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ closed-form evaluations.

\subsection{The bulk-plus-spike diagnostic}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Estimate edge fractions $\widehat F(t_i)$ on a grid $t_1 < \cdots < t_m$.
  \item Invert each to obtain $\widehat b_{\mathrm{eff}}(t_i)$.
  \item Under the single-law hypothesis $\widehat b_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is constant up to
    noise; under the bulk-plus-spike hypothesis it is strictly decreasing in $t$
    (Corollary~\ref{cor:window} plus Theorem~\ref{thm:steepen}).
  \item Test monotone decrease, e.g.\ by a rank statistic, or by comparing left-half and
    full-window refits, whose difference is one-sided under the alternative.
\end{enumerate}
The test targets a shape invariant, which by Theorem~\ref{thm:nonfals} no single window
can supply.

\subsection{Weight estimation with a censored spike exponent}
Given a bulk estimate $\widehat b_1$ and an edge fraction at a small window $t$, set
\[
  \widehat w = \frac{\widehat F(t) - F(\widehat b_1,t)}{1 - F(\widehat b_1,t)},
\]
the narrow-spike-limit estimator of Theorem~\ref{thm:spikeweight}; it deliberately does
not attempt to estimate $b_2$. A lower bound for $b_2$ is the smallest value for which
the two-component fit stays within the confidence band of the data.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What has been established}
A single edge-mass number is never decisive (Theorem~\ref{thm:nonfals}); if the truth is
a genuine mixture, no power law describes it on any window
(Theorems~\ref{thm:logconv},~\ref{thm:nosingle}); every single-law fit returns a
compromise exponent that drifts, and drifts upward as the window narrows to the left
(Theorems~\ref{thm:inflation},~\ref{thm:cumsep},~\ref{thm:steepen}); and the spike's
weight is estimable while its sharpness, past a threshold, is not
(Theorem~\ref{thm:spikeweight}). Each is a statement about the analytic families
themselves, independent of sample size, binning or estimator.

\subsection{Reinterpreting the canonical exponent}
The description $T(x) \propto (1+x)^{-1.104}$ is retired as the \emph{form} of the
profile and retained only as a pooled summary: by Theorem~\ref{thm:inflation} it is
exactly the effective compromise generated by a flat bulk and a narrow spike. The
canonical description becomes
\[
  T(x) = A(1+x)^{-b_{\mathrm{bulk}}} + K(1+x)^{-b_{\mathrm{edge}}},
  \qquad b_{\mathrm{bulk}} \approx 0.57,\quad b_{\mathrm{edge}} \gtrsim 10,
  \quad w \approx 0.09 .
\]

\subsection{Censoring and definitional drift}
An estimator reporting a parameter pinned at the boundary of its admissible range is
reporting censoring, not an estimate; Theorem~\ref{thm:spikeweight} identifies exactly
which parameter suffers this and which does not. Separately, every quantity here is
defined relative to the normalisation \eqref{eq:norm} and the one-sided window $[0,t]$.
Edge fractions computed under a different convention --- a combined two-sided edge, a
per-window equal-mean pooling, a logarithmic rescaling, or a different denominator in
\eqref{eq:norm} --- are different functionals and are not numerically comparable. In the
motivating dataset an earlier-quoted edge fraction of $0.2346$ is not reproducible under
the canonical convention, which yields $0.1620$; the leading explanation is a
definitional mismatch with a combined-edge decomposition (numerically $0.162+0.072$),
and the discrepancy requires reconciliation. No conclusion above depends on it: every
threshold is evaluated against the canonically measured $0.1620$. Edge statistics are
convention-sensitive in a way interior statistics are not.

\subsection{Scope}
The results are descriptive-form refinements inside the positional layer. They constrain
the shape of the positional profile and nothing else: no statement is made about
rate-level quantities or about structure orthogonal to position within a window.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Monotone drift of the fitted exponent]
For a mixture with $A,K>0$ and $b_1<b_2$, let $b_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)$ be the unique
exponent with $F(b_{\mathrm{eff}}(t),t) = M_w(b_1,b_2,t)$. Then $b_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is
strictly decreasing on $(0,1)$, with $b_{\mathrm{eff}}(t) \to b_2$ as $t \to 0^+$ and
tending to the pooled compromise value as $t \to 1^-$.
\end{conjecture}
The insight is that the local exponent of a two-component profile is a weighted average
of $b_1$ and $b_2$ whose weight is itself strictly decreasing in position, so every
cumulative statistic inherits the same drift; Theorem~\ref{thm:steepen} is the two-point
shadow of a genuinely monotone one-parameter family. Non-constancy is already proved;
the missing step is a derivative computation via the implicit function theorem applied
to $F$, whose strict monotonicity in the exponent supplies the required nondegeneracy.
Numerically the conjecture is clear: with $b_1 = 0.573$, $b_2 = 22.54$, $w = 0.086$, the
effective exponents at $t = 0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4,0.65,0.9,0.98$ are
$3.046, 2.591, 2.071, 1.524, 1.121, 0.945, 0.863, 0.846$.

\begin{conjecture}[Weight identifiable, exponent not --- quantitatively]
For fixed $b_1$ and $t$, the map $(w,b_2) \mapsto$ edge-fraction profile is not
injective: profiles with the same $w$ and different large $b_2$ differ in sup-distance
by $O(2^{-b_2})$, so $b_2$ is unidentifiable above a threshold while $w$ is determined
exactly by the $b_2 \to \infty$ limit of the excess over the bulk prediction.
\end{conjecture}
The convergence of Theorem~\ref{thm:spikeweight} should be uniform on compact windows,
making the family a compact perturbation of a one-parameter ($w$) family plus an
exponentially small remainder --- and that remainder, not noise, is what a fitting
procedure sees when it reports a censored spike exponent. Upgrading the pointwise limit
to a uniform statement with an explicit $2^{-b_2}$ rate requires only the closed form of
Theorem~\ref{thm:closed} and elementary bounds.

\begin{conjecture}[Two-window sufficiency]
Under a narrow-spike assumption, two well-separated windows suffice to identify
$(w,b_1)$: the map $(w,b_1) \mapsto \big(M_\infty(t_1), M_\infty(t_2)\big)$ is a
diffeomorphism onto its image for $t_1 \neq t_2$.
\end{conjecture}

Further directions: (a) a quantitative version of Theorem~\ref{thm:nosingle} lower
bounding the sup-distance between a genuine mixture and the best single power law on a
window of given width, in terms of $w$ and $b_2-b_1$, converting the qualitative no-go
into a power calculation; (b) extension of the rigidity theorem to general exponential
families of positional kernels --- the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:rigid} uses only that
the sufficient statistic $\log(1+x)$ is increasing, so the generalisation should cover
alternative shift and rescaling conventions; (c) a three-component analysis testing for
a right-edge feature, now that a directional diagnostic exists; (d) reconciliation of
edge-fraction conventions, with an explicit dictionary between combined-edge and
one-sided definitions.

\section{Conclusion}

A positional profile long summarised by a single power law with exponent $\approx 1.10$
is better described, decisively, as a nearly flat bulk plus a narrow left-edge spike.
The one-parameter family of harmonic-type kernels is rigid: its edge fraction is
strictly increasing in the exponent, so one measurement identifies one law. It is also
complete on the relevant range --- its edge fractions sweep out an entire interval up to
$1$ --- which is why no single measurement can falsify the family. Falsification requires
a shape invariant, and there is a clean one: pure power laws are multiplicatively affine
on geometric triples, while genuine two-component profiles are strictly multiplicatively
convex there. That gap propagates to densities, cumulative statistics and measured
log-log slopes alike, and it has a direction, steepening toward the left edge. What
remains unmeasurable is the sharpness of the spike, and the theory says precisely so:
above a resolution threshold the observable profile is flat in that parameter to
exponentially small order. The right summary is a bulk exponent, a weight, and a lower
bound.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core analytic objects
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def ker(b: float, x: float) -> float:
    """The positional kernel (1 + x)^(-b)."""
    return (1.0 + x) ** (-b)


def head_mass(b: float, t: float) -> float:
    """Closed form for int_0^t (1+x)^(-b) dx (with the b = 1 logarithmic case)."""
    if abs(b - 1.0) < 1e-14:
        import math

        return math.log(1.0 + t)
    return ((1.0 + t) ** (1.0 - b) - 1.0) / (1.0 - b)


def edge_frac(b: float, t: float) -> float:
    """Normalised cumulative mass F(b, t) = H(b, t) / H(b, 1)."""
    return head_mass(b, t) / head_mass(b, 1.0)


def quad(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, c: float, n: int = 200000) -> float:
    """Composite Simpson quadrature (n even), used only to check closed forms."""
    if n % 2 == 1:
        n += 1
    h = (c - a) / n
    total = f(a) + f(c)
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += (4.0 if i % 2 == 1 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return total * h / 3.0


def two_comp(A: float, K: float, b1: float, b2: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Two-component profile A (1+x)^(-b1) + K (1+x)^(-b2)."""
    return A * ker(b1, x) + K * ker(b2, x)


def mix_weight(A: float, K: float, b1: float, b2: float) -> float:
    """Relative total mass carried by the steep component."""
    m1 = A * head_mass(b1, 1.0)
    m2 = K * head_mass(b2, 1.0)
    return m2 / (m1 + m2)


def mix_frac(w: float, b1: float, b2: float, t: float) -> float:
    """Edge fraction of the two-point mixture."""
    return (1.0 - w) * edge_frac(b1, t) + w * edge_frac(b2, t)


def effective_exponent(target: float, t: float,
                       lo: float = -20.0, hi: float = 400.0,
                       tol: float = 1e-12) -> float:
    """Invert b |-> F(b, t) = target by bisection (well posed: F is strictly
    increasing in b, hence injective, for every interior t)."""
    for _ in range(400):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if edge_frac(mid, t) < target:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
        if hi - lo < tol:
            break
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


def local_exponent(f: Callable[[float], float], x: float, y: float) -> float:
    """Two-point log-log slope: -(log f(y) - log f(x)) / (log(1+y) - log(1+x))."""
    import math

    return -(math.log(f(y)) - math.log(f(x))) / (math.log(1.0 + y) - math.log(1.0 + x))


def geometric_triple(x0: float, x2: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Return (x0, x1, x2) with (1+x1)^2 = (1+x0)(1+x2)."""
    import math

    x1 = math.sqrt((1.0 + x0) * (1.0 + x2)) - 1.0
    return x0, x1, x2

def head_mass(b: float, t: float) -> float:
    """int_0^t (1+x)^(-b) dx, closed form (logarithmic at b = 1)."""
    import math
    if abs(b - 1.0) < 1e-14:

    return ((1.0 + t) ** (1.0 - b) - 1.0) / (1.0 - b)

def inverse_cdf_single(b: float, u: float) -> float:

    import math
    if abs(b - 1.0) < 1e-14:
        return math.exp(u * math.log(2.0)) - 1.0
    s = 1.0 - b
    return (1.0 + u * (2.0 ** s - 1.0)) ** (1.0 / s) - 1.0


def effective_exponent(target: float, t: float,
                       lo: float = -50.0, hi: float = 500.0) -> float:
    """Unique b with F(b, t) = target, by bisection."""
    for _ in range(300):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if edge_frac(mid, t) < target:
            lo = mid
        else:

    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)

class LCG:
    """Minimal linear congruential generator (Numerical-Recipes constants)."""

    def __init__(self, seed: int = 588) -> None:
        self.state = seed & 0xFFFFFFFF

    def uniform(self) -> float:
        self.state = (1664525 * self.state + 1013904223) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        return (self.state + 0.5) / 4294967296.0


def sample_mixture(n: int, w: float, b1: float, b2: float,
                   rng: LCG) -> List[float]:

    out: List[float] = []
    for _ in range(n):
        comp = b2 if rng.uniform() < w else b1
        out.append(inverse_cdf_single(comp, rng.uniform()))
    return out

    """Share of the sample lying in [0, t]."""
    return sum(1 for x in sample if x <= t) / len(sample)

        f = empirical_edge_frac(sample, t)
        f = min(max(f, 1e-6), 1.0 - 1e-6)
        rows.append((t, f, effective_exponent(f, t)))
    return rows

    """Kendall-type concordance score in [-1, 1] for the (t, b_eff) pairs.
    A value near -1 means strictly decreasing (bulk+spike signature); a value
    near 0 means no trend (single-law signature)."""
    conc = disc = 0
    m = len(rows)
    for i in range(m):
        for j in range(i + 1, m):

            if d > 0:

            elif d < 0:

    total = conc + disc
    return 0.0 if total == 0 else (conc - disc) / total

        else:

    return (observed_edge - bulk) / (1.0 - bulk)

                               weight: float, t: float,
                               tolerance: float,
                               b_max: float = 400.0) -> float:
    """Smallest spike exponent consistent with the data to within `tolerance`.

    converges to the narrow-spike limit, the set of admissible b2 is an upper
    ray, and its left endpoint is found by bisection. The routine returns that
    endpoint: values above it are statistically indistinguishable, so no point
    estimate is meaningful. Cost O(log(1/eps))."""
    def gap(b2: float) -> float:
        return abs(mix_frac(weight, bulk_exponent, b2, t) - observed_edge)

    if gap(hi) > tolerance:

    for _ in range(200):

        if gap(mid) > tolerance:

        else:

    return hi

    w = spike_weight(observed_edge, bulk_exponent, t)
    lb = spike_exponent_lower_bound(observed_edge, bulk_exponent, w, t, tolerance)
    plateau: List[Tuple[float, float]] = [

        "spike_weight": w,

        "spike_exponent_point_estimate": None,  # deliberately not identified

    """How the recovered weight depends on the assumed bulk exponent."""
    return [(b1, spike_weight(observed_edge, b1, t)) for b1 in bulk_grid]

def head_mass(b: float, t: float) -> float:

        return float(np.log1p(t))
    return ((1.0 + t) ** (1.0 - b) - 1.0) / (1.0 - b)


def edge_frac(b: float, t: float) -> float:
    return head_mass(b, t) / head_mass(b, 1.0)


def mix_frac(w: float, b1: float, b2: float, t: float) -> float:
    return (1 - w) * edge_frac(b1, t) + w * edge_frac(b2, t)


def effective_exponent(target: float, t: float) -> float:
    lo, hi = -60.0, 600.0
    for _ in range(300):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if edge_frac(mid, t) < target:
            lo = mid
        else:

def two_comp(A: float, K: float, b1: float, b2: float, x: float) -> float:
    return A * (1 + x) ** (-b1) + K * (1 + x) ** (-b2)


def local_exponent(f, x: float, y: float) -> float:
    return -(np.log(f(y)) - np.log(f(x))) / (np.log1p(y) - np.log1p(x))

      exponent you started with. Falsification has to come from a <em>shape</em> comparison, which

  </details>

  "interactive_layout": "# The Spike at the Edge

### A guided tour of what a fitted exponent is really telling you

---

## 1. A number that would not sit still

Rescale every observation window to the unit interval, pool thousands of hits, and histogram them. You get a shape. For a long time this particular shape had a name and a number: a decaying power law,

$$T(x) \;\propto\; (1+x)^{-1.104}, \qquad x \in [0,1].$$

The fits were good. The exponent was reproducible. And then somebody computed what that law predicts for the *left decile* — the share of all mass in the first tenth of the window. The prediction is $14.15\%$. The measurement, over nearly ten thousand pooled observations, is $16.20\%$, with an interval of $[15.47\%, 16.95\%]$.

Two percentage points. Signal, or artefact?

By the end of this page you will know not just the answer but *why the question was hard* — and you will have discovered the key obstruction yourself, by dragging a slider.

---

## 2. The object: a kernel and a fraction

Everything here revolves around one function, the **harmonic-type positional kernel**

$$\kappa_b(x) \;=\; (1+x)^{-b}, \qquad x \in [0,1].$$

The shift by $1$ matters: it keeps the profile finite at the left endpoint, so the family runs smoothly from flat ($b=0$) to arbitrarily concentrated ($b\to\infty$) without ever blowing up.

What one actually measures is not the kernel but its normalised cumulative mass, the **edge fraction**

$$F(b,t) \;=\; \frac{\int_0^t (1+x)^{-b}\,dx}{\int_0^1 (1+x)^{-b}\,dx}.$$

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the closed form (and why there are no integrals left)</summary>

For $b \ne 1$ the antiderivative of $(1+x)^{-b}$ is $\big((1+x)^{1-b}-1\big)/(1-b)$, so

$$\int_0^t (1+x)^{-b}\,dx \;=\; \frac{(1+t)^{1-b}-1}{1-b}, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad F(b,t) \;=\; \frac{(1+t)^{1-b}-1}{2^{\,1-b}-1},$$

the factor $1-b$ cancelling between numerator and denominator. The excluded value $b=1$ is the logarithmic case, $\int_0^t = \log(1+t)$, and nothing below depends on it. The flat case is a useful anchor: $F(0,t)=t$ exactly, because a uniform profile puts a tenth of its mass in a tenth of the window.

Plugging in the historical exponent gives $F(1.104,\,0.1) = 0.14181\ldots$ — the number the measurement missed.
</details>

---

## 3. Play first, theorise later

Before any theorem, get your hands on the object. In the laboratory below you blend a **flat bulk** with a **narrow left-edge spike** and watch what a single power law reports when it is asked to describe the blend.

Three things to try, in order:

1. **Set the spike weight to zero.** Everything becomes a genuine power law. Note that the drift panel at the bottom goes perfectly flat — the fitted exponent is the same on every window. That is *scale-freeness*, the defining charm of a power law.
2. **Push the weight up to a few percent.** The drift panel is no longer flat: it rises steeply toward the left. You have just produced, by hand, the signature that no power law can imitate.
3. **Press "Sharpen the spike" and keep raising the spike exponent.** Watch the readouts stop moving. Past a threshold, the data cannot see the difference. Remember this — it is a theorem, not a numerical artefact, and we come back to it at the end.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

---

## 4. Rigidity: one number pins down one law

Here is the first structural fact.

> **Rigidity.** For every interior window $t \in (0,1)$, the map $b \mapsto F(b,t)$ is *strictly increasing*.

Steepen the exponent, and more mass moves left — always, without exception. It sounds obvious, but it is not free: $F$ is a *ratio* of two integrals, and steepening shrinks numerator and denominator alike.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the proof (a monotone-likelihood-ratio argument)</summary>

Raising the exponent from $b$ to $b+c$ multiplies the kernel pointwise by $\kappa_c(x) = (1+x)^{-c}$, which is decreasing in $x$. So on the head $[0,t]$ the discount factor is *at least* $\kappa_c(t)$:

$$\kappa_c(t)\,H(b,t) \;\le\; H(b+c,t), \qquad H(b,t) := \int_0^t \kappa_b .$$

On the tail $[t,1]$ the same comparison runs the other way, and *strictly*: split the tail at the midpoint $m=(t+1)/2$; on $[m,1]$ the factor is at most $\kappa_c(m) < \kappa_c(t)$, and that piece has positive mass, so

$$\Theta(b+c,t) \;<\; \kappa_c(t)\,\Theta(b,t), \qquad \Theta(b,t) := \int_t^1 \kappa_b .$$

Now $F = H/(H+\Theta)$, and the inequality $F(b,t) < F(b+c,t)$ is equivalent, after clearing positive denominators, to $H_1\Theta_2 < H_2\Theta_1$ — which is exactly what the two displays give when combined. The head is discounted less than the tail; the ratio must rise. $\blacksquare$

Two immediate corollaries: the map is **injective** (a single edge-mass measurement identifies the exponent), and comparing with the flat case $F(0,t)=t$ gives $F(b,t) > t$ for every $b>0$: *a decaying profile always over-weights its own left edge*.
</details>

---

## 5. Why one measurement can never settle it

Now the deflating counterpoint — and it is the reason the original discrepancy could not close the case.

> **Spike limit.** $F(b,t) \to 1$ as $b \to \infty$, for every fixed $t > 0$.
>
> **Non-falsifiability.** Hence for any reference law $b_0>1$ and any $\alpha$ with $F(b_0,t) < \alpha < 1$, there is an exponent $b > b_0$ with $F(b,t) = \alpha$ *exactly*.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the proof</summary>

From the closed form, as $b \to \infty$ the exponent $1-b \to -\infty$, so both $(1+t)^{1-b}$ and $2^{1-b}$ tend to $0$ (their bases exceed $1$). The quotient tends to $(0-1)/(0-1) = 1$. Since $F(\cdot,t)$ is also continuous on $(1,\infty)$ — the denominator $2^{1-b}-1$ never vanishes there — the intermediate value theorem applied on $[b_0,B]$ with $F(B,t)>\alpha$ delivers the claimed exponent. $\blacksquare$
</details>

So no measured edge fraction, however discrepant, is evidence *against a power law*. It is evidence against *that particular* power law. Concretely: the measured $16.20\%$ is reproduced to the digit by $b \approx 1.5698$. Confirm it yourself in the first block of the numerical tour below, which also verifies the closed forms against direct quadrature and exhibits the whole rigidity table.

{{demo:0}}

The moral for experimental design is sharp: to distinguish "a slightly steeper single law" from "something structurally different at the edge", you must compare *shapes across windows*. Which brings us to the obstruction.

---

## 6. The obstruction: strict log-convexity on geometric triples

Call $x_0 < x_1 < x_2$ a **geometric triple** when

$$(1+x_1)^2 = (1+x_0)(1+x_2),$$

i.e. when the three shifted coordinates form a geometric progression. On such a triple, every pure power law is *exactly* multiplicative: $\kappa_b(x_1)^2 = \kappa_b(x_0)\kappa_b(x_2)$, because a power law is log-affine in $\log(1+x)$ and the triple is equally spaced on that scale.

Now the two-component profile

$$T(x) \;=\; A(1+x)^{-b_1} + K(1+x)^{-b_2}, \qquad A,K>0,\; b_1 \ne b_2 .$$

> **Strict multiplicative convexity.** On *every* geometric triple, $T(x_1)^2 < T(x_0)T(x_2)$.
>
> **No-go theorem.** Consequently there are no constants $C,b$ with $T(x) = C(1+x)^{-b}$ on any nondegenerate interval $[s,e]$ — not globally, and not on any subwindow, however small.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the proof (a strict AM–GM in disguise)</summary>

Write $a = \kappa_{b_1}(x_0)$, $a' = \kappa_{b_1}(x_2)$, $k = \kappa_{b_2}(x_0)$, $k' = \kappa_{b_2}(x_2)$, $p = \kappa_{b_1}(x_1)$, $q = \kappa_{b_2}(x_1)$. Log-affinity of each component gives $p^2 = aa'$ and $q^2 = kk'$, so expanding the product,

$$T(x_0)T(x_2) - T(x_1)^2 \;=\; A^2\underbrace{(aa'-p^2)}_{=0} + K^2\underbrace{(kk'-q^2)}_{=0} + AK\big(ak' + ka' - 2pq\big) .$$

Everything reduces to the two cross terms. Their product is $(ak')(ka') = (aa')(kk') = (pq)^2$, so $pq$ is exactly their geometric mean; by the *strict* AM–GM inequality, $2pq < ak' + ka'$ as soon as the two cross terms are unequal. And they are: for $c_1 < c_2$,

$$\kappa_{c_1}(x_0)\kappa_{c_2}(x_2) < \kappa_{c_2}(x_0)\kappa_{c_1}(x_2),$$

since dividing through by $\kappa_{c_1}(x_0)\kappa_{c_1}(x_2)>0$ reduces the claim to $(1+x_2)^{-(c_2-c_1)} < (1+x_0)^{-(c_2-c_1)}$, true because $x_0 < x_2$ and the exponent is negative. So $b_1 \ne b_2$ forces a strict gap. $\blacksquare$

For the no-go theorem, take any $[s,e]$ and set $x_1 = \sqrt{(1+s)(1+e)}-1$, the geometric midpoint; then $(s,x_1,e)$ is a geometric triple inside the window, and the strict inequality contradicts the equality a power law would force.
</details>

You can watch this obstruction in the laboratory: the readout labelled "log-convexity gap" is exactly the normalised quantity $\big(T(0)T(1) - T(\sqrt2-1)^2\big)/T(\sqrt2-1)^2$ on the triple $(0, \sqrt2 - 1, 1)$. It is zero when the weight is zero, and strictly positive the instant you introduce a second component. That single number is the whole falsifiability story.

The picture below makes the same point geometrically — a power law is a straight line on log-log axes, and the mixture bends.

## 7. What a fitted exponent is actually reporting

Suppose you know none of this and simply fit one power law to bulk-plus-spike data. What number comes back?

First a bookkeeping identity: normalising a two-component profile makes it an honest **two-point mixture** of the normalised components,

$$\frac{\int_0^t T}{\int_0^1 T} \;=\; (1-w)F(b_1,t) + w\,F(b_2,t), \qquad w = \frac{K\int_0^1 \kappa_{b_2}}{A\int_0^1\kappa_{b_1} + K\int_0^1 \kappa_{b_2}},$$

where $w$ is simply the share of total mass carried by the spike. Four parameters collapse to three.

Because $F$ is strictly increasing in the exponent, the mixture's edge fraction is squeezed strictly between the two pure values — and therefore:

> **Effective-exponent inflation.** Any single exponent calibrated to the mixture on a fixed window satisfies $b_1 < b_{\mathrm{eff}} < b_2$: strictly steeper than the bulk, strictly flatter than the spike.

That is the mechanism behind the whole affair. A flat bulk near $0.57$ plus a razor-thin spike, pooled and fitted with one law, reports something near $1.1$. The canonical exponent was never a slope — it was a compromise.

And the compromise cannot hold still:

> **Window dependence.** No single exponent reproduces the mixture's edge fraction at all windows $t \in (0,1)$; since an effective exponent exists for each $t$ separately, the fitted exponent is a genuinely non-constant function of the fitting window.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the proof (differentiating a cumulative identity)</summary>

Suppose one exponent $b$ worked at every $t$. The cumulative identity can be differentiated in $t$ (each edge fraction has derivative $\kappa_\beta(t)/H(\beta,1)$, by the fundamental theorem of calculus), and derivatives of functions agreeing on a neighbourhood are equal. Differentiating gives

$$\frac{1-w}{H(b_1,1)}\kappa_{b_1}(t) + \frac{w}{H(b_2,1)}\kappa_{b_2}(t) \;=\; \frac{1}{H(b,1)}\kappa_b(t) \qquad\text{for all } t \in (0,1),$$

which says a genuine two-component *density* equals a rescaled single kernel on, say, $[\tfrac14,\tfrac34]$ — contradicting the no-go theorem of §6. $\blacksquare$

So the separation survives normalisation and integration: it is visible in cumulative statistics, which is what experimenters actually measure.
</details>

Finally, the drift has a **direction**. The exponent reported by a two-point log-log slope on $[x,y]$ is $-\big(\log T(y)-\log T(x)\big)/\big(\log(1+y)-\log(1+x)\big)$. For a pure power law this returns $b$ regardless of window. For a genuine mixture, on any geometric triple, the slope on the left half-window is *strictly steeper* than on the right half — an immediate consequence of §6, since on a geometric triple the two log-spacings are equal and strict log-convexity says exactly $2\log T(x_1) < \log T(x_0) + \log T(x_2)$.

{{visualization:1}}

## 8. Turning theory into a test

The theorems dictate the experimental design. A one-window test is provably powerless (§5); a shape test is provably decisive (§6–§7). Here is the pipeline.

**Step one: invert the edge fraction.** Rigidity makes $F(\cdot,t)$ strictly increasing, and the spike limit makes its range all of $(0,1)$ — so bisection always works, needs no derivative and no starting guess, and cannot converge to the wrong root.

{{algorithm:0}}

**Step two: read off the exponent profile and test it for drift.** Under the single-law hypothesis the profile is flat up to noise; under the alternative it decreases, and only decreases.

{{algorithm:1}}

Does it work on data? The recovery experiment below generates positions from a known mixture by exact inverse-CDF sampling, throws the truth away, and runs the diagnostic blind — alongside a control sample drawn from a genuine single power law. The mixture yields a perfectly decreasing exponent profile; the control yields a flat one, spread under $0.04$. Precisely as the theory predicts, and precisely the pattern seen in the real data, where a left-half refit steepens the reported exponent from about $1.10$ to about $1.80$.

{{demo:1}}

---

## 9. What you can measure, and what you cannot

One last theorem, and it is a warning label. As the spike sharpens without bound,

$$(1-w)F(b_1,t) + w\,F(b_2,t) \;\longrightarrow\; (1-w)F(b_1,t) + w .$$

The limit does not involve $b_2$ at all. So:

* the **weight** $w$ is identified — it is exactly the excess of the measured edge mass over the bulk prediction, normalised by the largest possible excess;
* the **sharpness** $b_2$ is not — once the spike is narrower than your resolution, all sufficiently steep spikes look the same. At $t = 0.1$ with weight $0.086$ and bulk $0.573$, the mixture edge fractions for $b_2 = 50$ and $b_2 = 2000$ are $0.19542$ and $0.19622$: a difference in the fourth decimal.

You found this yourself in §3, by pushing the spike slider and watching the numbers freeze.

This is why an honest analysis reports a *lower bound* on the spike exponent together with a *point estimate of the weight* — and never the reverse. The estimator below does exactly that, and returns an explicit null in place of a point estimate for the sharpness.

{{algorithm:2}}

## 10. What changes

Three things.

**The canonical form.** The description "$T(x) \propto (1+x)^{-1.104}$" is retired as the *form* of this profile and retained only as a pooled summary statistic. The canonical description is now a nearly flat bulk with exponent around $0.57$ plus a narrow left-edge spike, steeper than about $10$, carrying a few percent of the mass. Applied to matched control data, the same two-component fit finds no spike at all — so the feature is not an artefact of the rescaling or the binning.

**The attribution.** More than half of the improvement in fit lives in the first decile alone, and essentially none of it near the interior features of the profile. The spike is a boundary phenomenon, orthogonal to whatever else happens in the middle of the window.

**The constraint.** A pure power law is now *known wrong* here, structurally and at every scale. Any future shape model must fail log-affinity on geometric triples. That is a falsifiable constraint, and it came not from more data but from knowing exactly what a two-parameter family can and cannot do.

There is a moral in the arithmetic. What made a two-percentage-point mismatch decidable was not a bigger sample. It was knowing, in advance and with proof, that a single number can never refute a power law, that a mixture can never *be* one on any window, and that a mixture's fitted exponent must drift steeper toward the edge. Once you know which measurements carry information, the data has no room left to be ambiguous.

/-!
# Separation of the bulk+spike profile from every single power law

`Pythagorean.EdgeKernelRefinement` proved that a two-component positional profile is not a
rescaled single power law *as a density*. This file upgrades the statement in two ways.

1. **Multiplicative strict convexity** (`twoComp_mul_gt_sq`). For every geometric triple
   `1+x₀, 1+x₁, 1+x₂` (i.e. `(1+x₁)² = (1+x₀)(1+x₂)`) a genuine two-component profile
   satisfies the *strict* inequality `f(x₁)² < f(x₀) f(x₂)`, whereas every pure power law
   satisfies it with equality. Consequently no single power law can match a bulk+spike
   profile on *any* nondegenerate subwindow (`twoComp_ne_single_on`) — not just globally.

2. **Cumulative (measurable) level** (`mixFrac_ne_single`). Even the *normalised cumulative*
   statistic separates the families: no exponent `b` reproduces the mixture's edge fraction
   simultaneously at all windows `t ∈ (0,1)`. Since an effective exponent does exist for each
   individual window (`exists_effective_exponent`), the fitted exponent is necessarily
   **window dependent** (`effective_exponent_window_dependent`): fitting the same profile on
   a narrower left window returns a different (steeper) exponent. This is the formal content
   of a "left-half refit steepens the fitted law" observation.

3. **Direction of the drift** (`localExponent_strictAnti`). The exponent reported by a
   log-log slope measurement is *strictly larger on the left half* of any geometric triple
   than on the right half, whereas a pure power law reports the same exponent everywhere
   (`localExponent_single`). So the drift is not merely nonconstant: it steepens toward the
   left edge.
-/

namespace Pythagorean.EdgeKernel

open MeasureTheory Filter Topology

/-! ## Multiplicative strict convexity of a two-component profile -/

/-- Auxiliary: on a geometric triple of bases the kernel is multiplicatively affine. -/
lemma ker_geom (β : ℝ) {x₀ x₁ x₂ : ℝ} (h₀ : 0 ≤ x₀) (h₂ : 0 ≤ x₂)
    (hgeom : (1 + x₁) ^ 2 = (1 + x₀) * (1 + x₂)) (hx₁ : 0 ≤ x₁) :
    ker β x₁ * ker β x₁ = ker β x₀ * ker β x₂ := by
  have hu : (0:ℝ) ≤ 1 + x₀ := by linarith
  have hv : (0:ℝ) ≤ 1 + x₂ := by linarith
  have hm : (1 + x₁) * (1 + x₁) = (1 + x₀) * (1 + x₂) := by nlinarith [hgeom]
  rw [ker, ker, ker, ← Real.mul_rpow (by linarith) (by linarith),
    ← Real.mul_rpow hu hv, hm]

/-- **Strict multiplicative convexity.** On any geometric triple of positions a genuine
two-component profile is strictly log-convex, while a pure power law is log-affine. -/
theorem twoComp_mul_gt_sq {A K b₁ b₂ x₀ x₁ x₂ : ℝ} (hA : 0 < A) (hK : 0 < K) (hb : b₁ ≠ b₂)
    (h₀ : 0 ≤ x₀) (h01 : x₀ < x₁) (h12 : x₁ < x₂)
    (hgeom : (1 + x₁) ^ 2 = (1 + x₀) * (1 + x₂)) :
    twoComp A K b₁ b₂ x₁ * twoComp A K b₁ b₂ x₁
      < twoComp A K b₁ b₂ x₀ * twoComp A K b₁ b₂ x₂ := by
  have hx₁ : 0 ≤ x₁ := le_trans h₀ h01.le
  have hx₂ : 0 ≤ x₂ := le_trans hx₁ h12.le
  have hu : (0:ℝ) < 1 + x₀ := by linarith
  have hv : (0:ℝ) < 1 + x₂ := by linarith
  -- abbreviations
  set a := ker b₁ x₀ with ha
  set a' := ker b₁ x₂ with ha'
  set k := ker b₂ x₀ with hk
  set k' := ker b₂ x₂ with hk'
  set p := ker b₁ x₁ with hp
  set q := ker b₂ x₁ with hq
  have hpp : p * p = a * a' := ker_geom b₁ h₀ hx₂ hgeom hx₁
  have hqq : q * q = k * k' := ker_geom b₂ h₀ hx₂ hgeom hx₁
  have hppos : 0 < p := ker_pos b₁ hx₁
  have hqpos : 0 < q := ker_pos b₂ hx₁
  -- the two cross terms have the same product as `(p*q)^2` but are distinct
  have hcross : (a * k') * (k * a') = (p * q) * (p * q) := by
    calc (a * k') * (k * a') = (a * a') * (k * k') := by ring
      _ = (p * p) * (q * q) := by rw [hpp, hqq]
      _ = (p * q) * (p * q) := by ring
  have hne : a * k' ≠ k * a' := by
    -- strict comparison of the two cross terms, by the sign of `b₂ - b₁`
    have key : ∀ c₁ c₂ : ℝ, c₁ < c₂ →
        ker c₁ x₀ * ker c₂ x₂ < ker c₂ x₀ * ker c₁ x₂ := by
      intro c₁ c₂ hlt
      have hd : (0:ℝ) < c₂ - c₁ := by linarith
      have hbase : (1 + x₂) ^ (-(c₂ - c₁)) < (1 + x₀) ^ (-(c₂ - c₁)) :=
        Real.rpow_lt_rpow_of_neg hu (by linarith) (by linarith)
      have hposmul : 0 < (1 + x₀) ^ (-c₁) * (1 + x₂) ^ (-c₁) := by
        exact mul_pos (Real.rpow_pos_of_pos hu _) (Real.rpow_pos_of_pos hv _)
      have hmul := mul_lt_mul_of_pos_right hbase hposmul
      have e1 : (1 + x₀) ^ (-(c₂ - c₁)) * ((1 + x₀) ^ (-c₁) * (1 + x₂) ^ (-c₁))
          = ker c₂ x₀ * ker c₁ x₂ := by
        rw [ker, ker, ← mul_assoc, ← Real.rpow_add hu]
        ring_nf
      have e2 : (1 + x₂) ^ (-(c₂ - c₁)) * ((1 + x₀) ^ (-c₁) * (1 + x₂) ^ (-c₁))
          = ker c₁ x₀ * ker c₂ x₂ := by
        rw [ker, ker]
        rw [show (1 + x₂) ^ (-(c₂ - c₁)) * ((1 + x₀) ^ (-c₁) * (1 + x₂) ^ (-c₁))
            = (1 + x₀) ^ (-c₁) * ((1 + x₂) ^ (-(c₂ - c₁)) * (1 + x₂) ^ (-c₁)) by ring,
          ← Real.rpow_add hv]
        ring_nf
      rw [e1, e2] at hmul
      exact hmul
    rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne hb with hlt | hgt
    · exact ne_of_lt (key b₁ b₂ hlt)
    · exact ne_of_gt (key b₂ b₁ hgt)
  -- AM-GM, strict because the cross terms differ
  have hPpos : 0 < a * k' := mul_pos (ker_pos b₁ h₀) (ker_pos b₂ hx₂)
  have hQpos : 0 < k * a' := mul_pos (ker_pos b₂ h₀) (ker_pos b₁ hx₂)
  have hAM : 2 * (p * q) < a * k' + k * a' := by
    have hsq : 0 < (a * k' - k * a') ^ 2 := by
      have : a * k' - k * a' ≠ 0 := sub_ne_zero.mpr hne
      positivity
    nlinarith [hcross, mul_pos hppos hqpos, hPpos, hQpos]
  simp only [twoComp, ← ha, ← ha', ← hk, ← hk', ← hp, ← hq]
  have key : (A * a + K * k) * (A * a' + K * k') - (A * p + K * q) * (A * p + K * q)
      = A * K * (a * k' + k * a' - 2 * (p * q)) := by
    linear_combination (-A ^ 2) * hpp - K ^ 2 * hqq
  nlinarith [key, hAM, mul_pos hA hK]

/-- **No single power law on any subwindow.** A genuine two-component profile disagrees with
every rescaled single kernel already on an arbitrary nondegenerate subwindow `[s,e]`. -/
theorem twoComp_ne_single_on {A K b₁ b₂ s e : ℝ} (hA : 0 < A) (hK : 0 < K) (hb : b₁ ≠ b₂)
    (hs : 0 ≤ s) (hse : s < e) :
    ¬ ∃ C b : ℝ, ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc s e, twoComp A K b₁ b₂ x = C * ker b x := by
  rintro ⟨C, b, h⟩
  have hu : (0:ℝ) < 1 + s := by linarith
  have hv : (0:ℝ) < 1 + e := by linarith
  set m : ℝ := Real.sqrt ((1 + s) * (1 + e)) with hm
  have hmsq : m ^ 2 = (1 + s) * (1 + e) := Real.sq_sqrt (by positivity)
  have hmu : 1 + s < m := by
    have : Real.sqrt ((1 + s) * (1 + s)) < Real.sqrt ((1 + s) * (1 + e)) :=
      Real.sqrt_lt_sqrt (by positivity) (by nlinarith)
    rwa [show (1 + s) * (1 + s) = (1 + s) ^ 2 by ring, Real.sqrt_sq (le_of_lt hu)] at this
  have hmv : m < 1 + e := by
    have : Real.sqrt ((1 + s) * (1 + e)) < Real.sqrt ((1 + e) * (1 + e)) :=
      Real.sqrt_lt_sqrt (by positivity) (by nlinarith)
    rwa [show (1 + e) * (1 + e) = (1 + e) ^ 2 by ring, Real.sqrt_sq (le_of_lt hv)] at this
  -- the middle point of the geometric triple
  set x₁ : ℝ := m - 1 with hx₁
  have hgeom : (1 + x₁) ^ 2 = (1 + s) * (1 + e) := by
    rw [hx₁]; simpa using hmsq
  have hstrict := twoComp_mul_gt_sq (A := A) (K := K) (b₁ := b₁) (b₂ := b₂)
    (x₀ := s) (x₁ := x₁) (x₂ := e) hA hK hb hs (by rw [hx₁]; linarith)
    (by rw [hx₁]; linarith) hgeom
  -- but the single law is multiplicatively affine on the same triple
  have hs' := h s ⟨le_rfl, hse.le⟩
  have he' := h e ⟨hse.le, le_rfl⟩
  have hm' := h x₁ ⟨by rw [hx₁]; linarith, by rw [hx₁]; linarith⟩
  have hkg : ker b x₁ * ker b x₁ = ker b s * ker b e :=
    ker_geom b hs (by linarith) hgeom (by rw [hx₁]; linarith)
  rw [hs', he', hm'] at hstrict
  have : C * ker b x₁ * (C * ker b x₁) = C * ker b s * (C * ker b e) := by
    linear_combination C ^ 2 * hkg
  linarith

/-! ## Window dependence of the fitted exponent -/

lemma hasDerivAt_headMass (b : ℝ) {t : ℝ} (ht0 : 0 < t) :
    HasDerivAt (fun s => headMass b s) (ker b t) t := by
  have hcont : ContinuousAt (ker b) t :=
    ContinuousAt.rpow_const (by fun_prop) (Or.inl (by linarith))
  have hmeasf : Measurable (ker b) := by unfold ker; fun_prop
  exact intervalIntegral.integral_hasDerivAt_right (ker_int b le_rfl ht0.le)
    ⟨Set.univ, Filter.univ_mem, hmeasf.aestronglyMeasurable⟩ hcont

lemma hasDerivAt_edgeFrac (β : ℝ) {t : ℝ} (ht0 : 0 < t) :
    HasDerivAt (fun s => edgeFrac β s) (ker β t / headMass β 1) t :=
  (hasDerivAt_headMass β ht0).div_const _

/-- **The cumulative statistic separates the families.** No single exponent reproduces the
edge fraction of a genuine bulk+spike mixture at all windows simultaneously. -/
theorem mixFrac_ne_single {w b₁ b₂ : ℝ} (hw0 : 0 < w) (hw1 : w < 1) (hb : b₁ ≠ b₂) :
    ¬ ∃ b : ℝ, ∀ t ∈ Set.Ioo (0:ℝ) 1, mixFrac w b₁ b₂ t = edgeFrac b t := by
  rintro ⟨b, h⟩
  have hH₁ : 0 < headMass b₁ 1 := headMass_pos b₁ one_pos
  have hH₂ : 0 < headMass b₂ 1 := headMass_pos b₂ one_pos
  have hHb : 0 < headMass b 1 := headMass_pos b one_pos
  set A : ℝ := (1 - w) / headMass b₁ 1 with hA
  set K : ℝ := w / headMass b₂ 1 with hK
  have hApos : 0 < A := by rw [hA]; exact div_pos (by linarith) hH₁
  have hKpos : 0 < K := by rw [hK]; exact div_pos hw0 hH₂
  -- differentiate the assumed identity on the open window
  have hderiv : ∀ t ∈ Set.Ioo (0:ℝ) 1,
      twoComp A K b₁ b₂ t = (1 / headMass b 1) * ker b t := by
    intro t ht
    have hmix : HasDerivAt (fun s => mixFrac w b₁ b₂ s) (A * ker b₁ t + K * ker b₂ t) t := by
      have d₁ := (hasDerivAt_edgeFrac b₁ ht.1).const_mul (1 - w)
      have d₂ := (hasDerivAt_edgeFrac b₂ ht.1).const_mul w
      have hsum := d₁.add d₂
      have hfun : (fun s => mixFrac w b₁ b₂ s)
          = fun s => (1 - w) * edgeFrac b₁ s + w * edgeFrac b₂ s := rfl
      rw [hfun]
      convert hsum using 1
      rw [hA, hK]; ring
    have hsingle : HasDerivAt (fun s => edgeFrac b s) ((1 / headMass b 1) * ker b t) t := by
      have hd := hasDerivAt_edgeFrac b ht.1
      convert hd using 1
      ring
    have heq : (fun s => mixFrac w b₁ b₂ s) =ᶠ[𝓝 t] fun s => edgeFrac b s := by
      filter_upwards [Ioo_mem_nhds ht.1 ht.2] with s hs using h s hs
    have := (hmix.congr_of_eventuallyEq heq.symm).unique hsingle
    simpa [twoComp] using this
  -- and contradict the subwindow separation
  refine twoComp_ne_single_on (A := A) (K := K) (b₁ := b₁) (b₂ := b₂)
    (s := 1/4) (e := 3/4) hApos hKpos hb (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
    ⟨1 / headMass b 1, b, ?_⟩
  intro x hx
  exact hderiv x ⟨by linarith [hx.1], by linarith [hx.2]⟩

/-- For each individual window an effective exponent does exist (and is steeper than the
bulk): the mixture's edge fraction is realised by a single law window by window. -/
theorem exists_effective_exponent {w b₁ b₂ t : ℝ} (hw0 : 0 < w) (hw1 : w < 1)
    (hb₁ : 1 < b₁) (hb : b₁ < b₂) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1) :
    ∃ b, b₁ < b ∧ edgeFrac b t = mixFrac w b₁ b₂ t := by
  refine exists_edgeFrac_eq ht0 hb₁ (mixFrac_gt_bulk hw0 hb ht0 ht1) ?_
  have h₁ := edgeFrac_lt_one b₁ ht0.le ht1
  have h₂ := edgeFrac_lt_one b₂ ht0.le ht1
  rw [mixFrac]
  nlinarith

/-- **Window dependence of the fitted exponent.** If a single-law exponent is fitted to the
mixture window by window, the resulting exponent cannot be constant: refitting on a different
window necessarily returns a different exponent. -/
theorem effective_exponent_window_dependent {w b₁ b₂ : ℝ} (hw0 : 0 < w) (hw1 : w < 1)
    (hb : b₁ ≠ b₂) (beff : ℝ → ℝ)
    (hfit : ∀ t ∈ Set.Ioo (0:ℝ) 1, edgeFrac (beff t) t = mixFrac w b₁ b₂ t) :
    ¬ ∃ c, ∀ t ∈ Set.Ioo (0:ℝ) 1, beff t = c := by
  rintro ⟨c, hc⟩
  refine mixFrac_ne_single hw0 hw1 hb ⟨c, fun t ht => ?_⟩
  have := hfit t ht
  rwa [hc t ht, eq_comm] at this


/-! ## The measured local exponent steepens toward the left edge -/

/-- The exponent that a two-point (log-log) slope measurement on the window `[x,y]` reports
for a profile `f`. -/
noncomputable def localExponent (f : ℝ → ℝ) (x y : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  -(Real.log (f y) - Real.log (f x)) / (Real.log (1 + y) - Real.log (1 + x))

/-- A pure power law reports the same exponent on every window: the slope measurement is
scale free. -/
theorem localExponent_single {C b x y : ℝ} (hC : 0 < C) (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hxy : x < y) :
    localExponent (fun z => C * ker b z) x y = b := by
  have hx1 : (0:ℝ) < 1 + x := by linarith
  have hy1 : (0:ℝ) < 1 + y := by linarith
  have hd : Real.log (1 + x) < Real.log (1 + y) := Real.log_lt_log hx1 (by linarith)
  have hlog : ∀ z : ℝ, 0 ≤ z → Real.log (C * ker b z) = Real.log C - b * Real.log (1 + z) := by
    intro z hz
    have hz1 : (0:ℝ) < 1 + z := by linarith
    rw [Real.log_mul (ne_of_gt hC) (ne_of_gt (ker_pos _ hz)), ker, Real.log_rpow hz1]
    ring
  have hne : Real.log (1 + y) - Real.log (1 + x) ≠ 0 := sub_ne_zero.mpr (ne_of_gt hd)
  rw [localExponent, hlog x hx, hlog y (by linarith), div_eq_iff hne]
  ring

/-- **Left-edge steepening.** On a geometric triple of positions, a genuine two-component
profile reports a strictly steeper exponent on the left half-window than on the right
half-window. A pure power law reports the same exponent on both. -/
theorem localExponent_strictAnti {A K b₁ b₂ x₀ x₁ x₂ : ℝ} (hA : 0 < A) (hK : 0 < K)
    (hb : b₁ ≠ b₂) (h₀ : 0 ≤ x₀) (h01 : x₀ < x₁) (h12 : x₁ < x₂)
    (hgeom : (1 + x₁) ^ 2 = (1 + x₀) * (1 + x₂)) :
    localExponent (twoComp A K b₁ b₂) x₁ x₂ < localExponent (twoComp A K b₁ b₂) x₀ x₁ := by
  have hx₁ : 0 ≤ x₁ := le_trans h₀ h01.le
  have hx₂ : 0 ≤ x₂ := le_trans hx₁ h12.le
  have hu : (0:ℝ) < 1 + x₀ := by linarith
  have hm : (0:ℝ) < 1 + x₁ := by linarith
  have hv : (0:ℝ) < 1 + x₂ := by linarith
  have hfpos : ∀ z : ℝ, 0 ≤ z → 0 < twoComp A K b₁ b₂ z := by
    intro z hz
    have := ker_pos b₁ hz
    have := ker_pos b₂ hz
    unfold twoComp
    positivity
  -- the two log-spacings agree
  have hspace : Real.log (1 + x₁) - Real.log (1 + x₀) = Real.log (1 + x₂) - Real.log (1 + x₁) := by
    have h2 : Real.log ((1 + x₁) * (1 + x₁)) = Real.log ((1 + x₀) * (1 + x₂)) := by
      rw [show (1 + x₁) * (1 + x₁) = (1 + x₁) ^ 2 by ring, hgeom]
    rw [Real.log_mul (ne_of_gt hm) (ne_of_gt hm), Real.log_mul (ne_of_gt hu) (ne_of_gt hv)] at h2
    linarith

namespace Pythagorean.EdgeKernel

open MeasureTheory intervalIntegral Filter Topology

/-! ## The harmonic-type kernel and its cumulative mass -/

/-- The positional kernel `x ↦ (1+x)^{-b}` on the normalised window. -/
noncomputable def ker (b x : ℝ) : ℝ := (1 + x) ^ (-b)

@[simp] lemma ker_zero_arg (b : ℝ) : ker b 0 = 1 := by
  simp [ker]

lemma ker_pos (b : ℝ) {x : ℝ} (hx : 0 ≤ x) : 0 < ker b x :=
  Real.rpow_pos_of_pos (by linarith) _

lemma ker_cont (b : ℝ) : ContinuousOn (ker b) (Set.Ici (0 : ℝ)) := by
  intro x hx
  simp only [Set.mem_Ici] at hx
  exact ContinuousAt.continuousWithinAt
    (ContinuousAt.rpow_const (by fun_prop) (Or.inl (by linarith)))

lemma ker_int (b : ℝ) {a c : ℝ} (ha : 0 ≤ a) (hc : 0 ≤ c) :
    IntervalIntegrable (ker b) volume a c := by
  apply ContinuousOn.intervalIntegrable
  refine (ker_cont b).mono ?_
  intro y hy
  rw [Set.mem_uIcc] at hy
  simp only [Set.mem_Ici]
  rcases hy with ⟨h1, h2⟩ | ⟨h1, h2⟩ <;> linarith

/-- Additivity of the exponent turns into multiplicativity of the kernel. -/
lemma ker_add_mul (b c : ℝ) {x : ℝ} (hx : 0 ≤ x) : ker (b + c) x = ker b x * ker c x := by
  rw [ker, ker, ker, ← Real.rpow_add (by linarith : (0:ℝ) < 1 + x)]
  ring_nf

/-- For a nonnegative exponent the kernel is antitone in the position. -/
lemma ker_antitone (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 ≤ c) {x y : ℝ} (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hxy : x ≤ y) :
    ker c y ≤ ker c x :=
  Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_nonpos (by linarith) (by linarith) (neg_nonpos.mpr hc)

/-- For a positive exponent the kernel is strictly antitone in the position. -/
lemma ker_strictAnti (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 < c) {x y : ℝ} (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hxy : x < y) :
    ker c y < ker c x :=
  Real.rpow_lt_rpow_of_neg (by linarith) (by linarith) (neg_neg_iff_pos.mpr hc)

/-- Mass of the kernel on the initial segment `[0,t]`. -/
noncomputable def headMass (b t : ℝ) : ℝ := ∫ x in (0:ℝ)..t, ker b x

/-- Mass of the kernel on the terminal segment `[t,1]`. -/
noncomputable def tailMass (b t : ℝ) : ℝ := ∫ x in t..(1:ℝ), ker b x

lemma headMass_pos (b : ℝ) {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) : 0 < headMass b t := by
  refine intervalIntegral.intervalIntegral_pos_of_pos_on (ker_int b le_rfl ht.le) ?_ ht
  intro x hx
  exact ker_pos b (le_of_lt (by simpa using hx.1))

lemma tailMass_pos (b : ℝ) {t : ℝ} (ht0 : 0 ≤ t) (ht : t < 1) : 0 < tailMass b t := by
  refine intervalIntegral.intervalIntegral_pos_of_pos_on (ker_int b ht0 zero_le_one) ?_ ht
  intro x hx
  exact ker_pos b (by linarith [hx.1])

lemma headMass_add_tailMass (b : ℝ) {t : ℝ} (ht0 : 0 ≤ t) :
    headMass b t + tailMass b t = headMass b 1 :=
  intervalIntegral.integral_add_adjacent_intervals (ker_int b le_rfl ht0)
    (ker_int b ht0 zero_le_one)

lemma hasDerivAt_headMass_antideriv (b : ℝ) (hb : b ≠ 1) {x : ℝ} (hx : 0 ≤ x) :
    HasDerivAt (fun y : ℝ => ((1 + y) ^ (1 - b) - 1) / (1 - b)) (ker b x) x := by
  have h1 : (1:ℝ) + x ≠ 0 := by linarith
  have hd : HasDerivAt (fun y : ℝ => (1 + y) ^ (1 - b)) ((1 - b) * (1 + x) ^ (1 - b - 1)) x := by
    have := (Real.hasDerivAt_rpow_const (p := 1 - b) (Or.inl h1)).comp x
      ((hasDerivAt_id x).const_add 1)
    simpa using this
  have hres := (hd.sub_const 1).div_const (1 - b)
  convert hres using 1
  have hb' : (1:ℝ) - b ≠ 0 := by intro h; apply hb; linarith
  field_simp [ker]
  ring_nf
  rfl

/-- Closed form for the cumulative kernel mass (the case `b ≠ 1`). -/
theorem headMass_eq (b : ℝ) (hb : b ≠ 1) {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    headMass b t = ((1 + t) ^ (1 - b) - 1) / (1 - b) := by
  have := intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt
    (f := fun y : ℝ => ((1 + y) ^ (1 - b) - 1) / (1 - b)) (f' := ker b) (a := 0) (b := t)
    (fun x hx => hasDerivAt_headMass_antideriv b hb
      (by rw [Set.uIcc_of_le ht] at hx; exact hx.1))
    (ker_int b le_rfl ht)
  simp [headMass, this]

@[simp] lemma headMass_zero_exp (t : ℝ) : headMass 0 t = t := by
  simp [headMass, ker]

/-! ## The normalised edge fraction -/

/-- Fraction of the kernel mass carried by the initial segment `[0,t]` of the window. -/
noncomputable def edgeFrac (b t : ℝ) : ℝ := headMass b t / headMass b 1

@[simp] lemma edgeFrac_zero_exp (t : ℝ) : edgeFrac 0 t = t := by
  simp [edgeFrac, headMass_zero_exp t, headMass_zero_exp 1]

lemma edgeFrac_pos (b : ℝ) {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) : 0 < edgeFrac b t :=
  div_pos (headMass_pos b ht) (headMass_pos b one_pos)

lemma edgeFrac_lt_one (b : ℝ) {t : ℝ} (ht0 : 0 ≤ t) (ht1 : t < 1) : edgeFrac b t < 1 := by
  rw [edgeFrac, div_lt_one (headMass_pos b one_pos), ← headMass_add_tailMass b ht0]
  linarith [tailMass_pos b ht0 ht1]

/-! ### Monotone likelihood ratio: rigidity of the single-law family -/

/-- On the head `[0,t]`, steepening the exponent by `c` costs at most the factor `ker c t`. -/
lemma headMass_le_of_add (b : ℝ) {c t : ℝ} (hc : 0 ≤ c) (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    ker c t * headMass b t ≤ headMass (b + c) t := by
  rw [headMass, headMass, ← intervalIntegral.integral_const_mul]
  refine intervalIntegral.integral_mono_on ht ((ker_int b le_rfl ht).const_mul _)
    (ker_int (b + c) le_rfl ht) ?_
  intro x hx
  have hx0 : 0 ≤ x := hx.1
  have h1 : ker c t ≤ ker c x := ker_antitone c hc hx0 hx.2
  rw [ker_add_mul b c hx0]
  nlinarith [ker_pos b hx0]

/-- On the tail `[t,1]`, steepening the exponent by `c` costs *strictly more* than `ker c t`. -/
lemma tailMass_lt_of_add (b : ℝ) {c t : ℝ} (hc : 0 < c) (ht0 : 0 ≤ t) (ht1 : t < 1) :
    tailMass (b + c) t < ker c t * tailMass b t := by
  set m : ℝ := (t + 1) / 2 with hm
  have htm : t < m := by rw [hm]; linarith
  have hm1 : m < 1 := by rw [hm]; linarith
  have hm0 : 0 ≤ m := by linarith
  have hsplit : ∀ b' : ℝ, tailMass b' t = (∫ x in t..m, ker b' x) + ∫ x in m..(1:ℝ), ker b' x := by
    intro b'
    exact (intervalIntegral.integral_add_adjacent_intervals (ker_int b' ht0 hm0)
      (ker_int b' hm0 zero_le_one)).symm
  have hA : (∫ x in t..m, ker (b + c) x) ≤ ker c t * ∫ x in t..m, ker b x := by
    rw [← intervalIntegral.integral_const_mul]
    refine intervalIntegral.integral_mono_on htm.le (ker_int (b + c) ht0 hm0)
      ((ker_int b ht0 hm0).const_mul _) ?_
    intro x hx
    have hx0 : 0 ≤ x := le_trans ht0 hx.1
    have h1 : ker c x ≤ ker c t := ker_antitone c hc.le ht0 hx.1
    rw [ker_add_mul b c hx0]
    nlinarith [ker_pos b hx0]
  have hB : (∫ x in m..(1:ℝ), ker (b + c) x) < ker c t * ∫ x in m..(1:ℝ), ker b x := by
    have hlt : ker c m < ker c t := ker_strictAnti c hc ht0 htm
    have h1 : (∫ x in m..(1:ℝ), ker (b + c) x) ≤ ker c m * ∫ x in m..(1:ℝ), ker b x := by
      rw [← intervalIntegral.integral_const_mul]
      refine intervalIntegral.integral_mono_on hm1.le (ker_int (b + c) hm0 zero_le_one)
        ((ker_int b hm0 zero_le_one).const_mul _) ?_
      intro x hx
      have hx0 : 0 ≤ x := le_trans hm0 hx.1
      have h1 : ker c x ≤ ker c m := ker_antitone c hc.le hm0 hx.1
      rw [ker_add_mul b c hx0]
      nlinarith [ker_pos b hx0]
    have hpos : 0 < ∫ x in m..(1:ℝ), ker b x :=
      intervalIntegral.intervalIntegral_pos_of_pos_on (ker_int b hm0 zero_le_one)
        (fun x hx => ker_pos b (by linarith [hx.1])) hm1
    nlinarith
  rw [hsplit (b + c), hsplit b]
  nlinarith

/-- **Rigidity.** For each interior `t` the edge fraction is a strictly increasing
function of the exponent. -/
theorem edgeFrac_strictMono {b₁ b₂ t : ℝ} (hb : b₁ < b₂) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1) :
    edgeFrac b₁ t < edgeFrac b₂ t := by
  obtain ⟨c, hc0, rfl⟩ : ∃ c, 0 < c ∧ b₂ = b₁ + c := ⟨b₂ - b₁, by linarith, by ring⟩
  have h1 := headMass_le_of_add b₁ hc0.le ht0.le
  have h2 := tailMass_lt_of_add b₁ hc0 ht0.le ht1
  have hH1 : 0 < headMass b₁ t := headMass_pos b₁ ht0
  have hH2 : 0 < headMass (b₁ + c) t := headMass_pos _ ht0
  have hT1 : 0 < tailMass b₁ t := tailMass_pos b₁ ht0.le ht1
  have hT2 : 0 < tailMass (b₁ + c) t := tailMass_pos _ ht0.le ht1
  rw [edgeFrac, edgeFrac, ← headMass_add_tailMass b₁ ht0.le,
    ← headMass_add_tailMass (b₁ + c) ht0.le,
    div_lt_div_iff₀ (by linarith) (by linarith)]
  nlinarith [ker_pos c ht0.le]

/-- The exponent is identified by a single edge-fraction measurement. -/
theorem edgeFrac_injective {t : ℝ} (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1) :
    Function.Injective (fun b => edgeFrac b t) := by
  intro b₁ b₂ h
  rcases lt_trichotomy b₁ b₂ with hlt | heq | hgt
  · exact absurd h (ne_of_lt (edgeFrac_strictMono hlt ht0 ht1))
  · exact heq
  · exact absurd h.symm (ne_of_lt (edgeFrac_strictMono hgt ht0 ht1))

/-- Any decreasing kernel over-weights the initial segment relative to its length. -/
theorem edgeFrac_gt_of_pos {b t : ℝ} (hb : 0 < b) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1) :
    t < edgeFrac b t := by
  have := edgeFrac_strictMono hb ht0 ht1
  rwa [edgeFrac_zero_exp t] at this

/-! ### The spike limit and non-falsifiability of a single measurement -/

/-- The closed form of the edge fraction in terms of the exponent (`b ≠ 1`). -/
theorem edgeFrac_eq (b : ℝ) (hb : b ≠ 1) {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    edgeFrac b t = ((1 + t) ^ (1 - b) - 1) / ((2 : ℝ) ^ (1 - b) - 1) := by
  have hb' : (1 : ℝ) - b ≠ 0 := fun h => hb (by linarith)
  have h1 : headMass b 1 = ((2 : ℝ) ^ (1 - b) - 1) / (1 - b) := by
    rw [headMass_eq b hb zero_le_one]; norm_num
  have hpos := headMass_pos b one_pos
  rw [h1] at hpos
  have hden : (2 : ℝ) ^ (1 - b) - 1 ≠ 0 := by
    intro h; rw [h] at hpos; simp at hpos
  rw [edgeFrac, h1, headMass_eq b hb ht]
  field_simp

/-- **Spike limit.** As the exponent grows, all the mass concentrates at the left edge. -/
theorem edgeFrac_tendsto_one {t : ℝ} (ht0 : 0 < t) :
    Tendsto (fun b => edgeFrac b t) atTop (𝓝 1) := by
  have hlin : Tendsto (fun b : ℝ => 1 - b) atTop atBot := by
    simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using tendsto_atBot_add_const_left atTop (1 : ℝ) tendsto_neg_atTop_atBot
  have h1 : Tendsto (fun b : ℝ => (1 + t) ^ (1 - b)) atTop (𝓝 0) :=
    (tendsto_rpow_atBot_of_base_gt_one (1 + t) (by linarith)).comp hlin
  have h2 : Tendsto (fun b : ℝ => (2 : ℝ) ^ (1 - b)) atTop (𝓝 0) :=
    (tendsto_rpow_atBot_of_base_gt_one 2 (by norm_num)).comp hlin
  have hq : Tendsto (fun b : ℝ => ((1 + t) ^ (1 - b) - 1) / ((2 : ℝ) ^ (1 - b) - 1)) atTop
      (𝓝 (((0 : ℝ) - 1) / ((0 : ℝ) - 1))) :=
    (h1.sub tendsto_const_nhds).div (h2.sub tendsto_const_nhds) (by norm_num)
  rw [show ((0 : ℝ) - 1) / ((0 : ℝ) - 1) = 1 by norm_num] at hq
  refine hq.congr' ?_
  filter_upwards [eventually_gt_atTop (1 : ℝ)] with b hb
  exact (edgeFrac_eq b (ne_of_gt hb) ht0.le).symm

/-- The edge fraction depends continuously on the exponent (on the range `b > 1`). -/
lemma edgeFrac_continuousOn {t : ℝ} (ht0 : 0 ≤ t) :
    ContinuousOn (fun b => edgeFrac b t) (Set.Ioi (1 : ℝ)) := by
  have hcong : Set.EqOn (fun b => edgeFrac b t)
      (fun b => ((1 + t) ^ (1 - b) - 1) / ((2 : ℝ) ^ (1 - b) - 1)) (Set.Ioi 1) :=
    fun b hb => edgeFrac_eq b (ne_of_gt (Set.mem_Ioi.mp hb)) ht0
  refine ContinuousOn.congr ?_ hcong
  have c1 : Continuous fun b : ℝ => (1 + t) ^ (1 - b) :=
    (continuous_iff_continuousAt.2 fun _ =>
      Real.continuousAt_const_rpow (a := 1 + t) (ne_of_gt (by linarith))).comp (by fun_prop)
  have c2 : Continuous fun b : ℝ => (2 : ℝ) ^ (1 - b) :=
    (continuous_iff_continuousAt.2 fun _ =>
      Real.continuousAt_const_rpow (a := 2) (by norm_num)).comp (by fun_prop)
  refine ((c1.sub continuous_const).continuousOn).div
    ((c2.sub continuous_const).continuousOn) ?_
  intro b hb
  have h : (2 : ℝ) ^ (1 - b) < 1 :=
    Real.rpow_lt_one_of_one_lt_of_neg (by norm_num) (by simp only [Set.mem_Ioi] at hb; linarith)
  intro hzero
  rw [sub_eq_zero] at hzero
  linarith

/-- **A single edge-mass number cannot refute a power law.** Every value above the edge
fraction of a given law (and below `1`) is realised by a steeper law. -/
theorem exists_edgeFrac_eq {t b₀ α : ℝ} (ht0 : 0 < t) (hb₀ : 1 < b₀)
    (hα₁ : edgeFrac b₀ t < α) (hα₂ : α < 1) :
    ∃ b, b₀ < b ∧ edgeFrac b t = α := by
  obtain ⟨B, hBα, hBb₀⟩ :
      ∃ B, α < edgeFrac B t ∧ b₀ < B := by
    have h := (edgeFrac_tendsto_one ht0).eventually (eventually_gt_nhds hα₂)
    obtain ⟨B, hB⟩ := (h.and (eventually_gt_atTop b₀)).exists
    exact ⟨B, hB.1, hB.2⟩
  have hsub : Set.Icc b₀ B ⊆ Set.Ioi (1 : ℝ) := fun x hx => lt_of_lt_of_le hb₀ hx.1
  have hcont : ContinuousOn (fun b => edgeFrac b t) (Set.Icc b₀ B) :=
    (edgeFrac_continuousOn ht0.le).mono hsub
  have hmem : α ∈ Set.Icc (edgeFrac b₀ t) (edgeFrac B t) := ⟨hα₁.le, hBα.le⟩
  obtain ⟨b, hbmem, hb⟩ := intermediate_value_Icc hBb₀.le hcont hmem
  refine ⟨b, ?_, hb⟩
  rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hbmem.1 with heq | hlt
  · exact absurd (heq ▸ hb) (ne_of_lt hα₁)
  · exact hlt

/-! ## Two-component profiles -/

/-- A two-component ("flat bulk + narrow edge spike") positional profile. -/
noncomputable def twoComp (A K b₁ b₂ x : ℝ) : ℝ := A * ker b₁ x + K * ker b₂ x

/-- **Falsifiability theorem.** A genuine two-component profile is not a pure power law:
no rescaled single kernel agrees with it on the three sample points `0`, `√2-1`, `1`. -/
theorem twoComp_ne_single {A K b₁ b₂ : ℝ} (hA : 0 < A) (hK : 0 < K) (hb : b₁ ≠ b₂) :
    ¬ ∃ C b : ℝ, ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, twoComp A K b₁ b₂ x = C * ker b x := by
  rintro ⟨C, b, h⟩
  have hs2 : (1 : ℝ) < Real.sqrt 2 := by
    have : Real.sqrt 1 < Real.sqrt 2 := Real.sqrt_lt_sqrt (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
    simpa using this
  have hs2' : Real.sqrt 2 ≤ 2 := by
    nlinarith [Real.sq_sqrt (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) ≤ 2), Real.sqrt_nonneg 2]
  set p : ℝ → ℝ := fun β => (Real.sqrt 2) ^ (-β) with hp
  have hkers : ∀ β : ℝ, ker β (Real.sqrt 2 - 1) = p β := by
    intro β; rw [ker, hp]; ring_nf
  have hker1 : ∀ β : ℝ, ker β 1 = p β * p β := by
    intro β
    rw [ker, hp, ← Real.mul_rpow (Real.sqrt_nonneg 2) (Real.sqrt_nonneg 2),
      Real.mul_self_sqrt (by norm_num)]
    norm_num
  have h0 := h 0 (by constructor <;> norm_num)
  have hmid := h (Real.sqrt 2 - 1) ⟨by linarith, by linarith⟩
  have h1 := h 1 (by constructor <;> norm_num)
  rw [twoComp, ker_zero_arg, ker_zero_arg, ker_zero_arg] at h0
  rw [twoComp, hkers, hkers, hkers] at hmid
  rw [twoComp, hker1, hker1, hker1] at h1
  have hC : A + K = C := by linarith
  have h3 : (A + K) * (A * p b₁ ^ 2 + K * p b₂ ^ 2) = (A * p b₁ + K * p b₂) ^ 2 := by
    calc (A + K) * (A * p b₁ ^ 2 + K * p b₂ ^ 2)
        = C * (A * (p b₁ * p b₁) + K * (p b₂ * p b₂)) := by rw [← hC]; ring
      _ = C * (C * (p b * p b)) := by rw [← h1]
      _ = (C * p b) * (C * p b) := by ring
      _ = (A * p b₁ + K * p b₂) * (A * p b₁ + K * p b₂) := by rw [← hmid]

        ker(b, x) = (1 + x) ** (-b),

its cumulative head mass

and the normalised *edge fraction*

        F(b, t) = H(b, t) / H(b, 1) = ((1+t)^(1-b) - 1) / (2^(1-b) - 1).

accompanying paper:

  2. rigidity: b |-> F(b, t) is strictly increasing, hence injective;
  3. left over-weighting: F(b, t) > t for b > 0;

  7. effective-exponent inflation: b_bulk < b_eff < b_edge;
